_about: Curated peg-break, near-miss and edge-case episodes. Narrative fields are summaries written for this tool; every quantitative claim in 'datapoints' carries its own source. Magnitudes shown in the app are computed from the price series, not from these notes. series.source: bis_d (BIS daily, local per USD), bis_m (BIS monthly average), yahoo (Yahoo Finance close; for pegged currencies usually reflects offshore dealer quotes). If anchor is given, the app shows local currency per unit of anchor. quote=per_anchor means the ticker is already quoted against the anchor.

episodes.title: Qatar 2017: onshore peg holds, offshore market breaks
episodes.regime_before: Hard peg at 3.64/USD (de facto since 1980, formal since 2001)
episodes.regime_after: Peg unchanged onshore; offshore quotes normalised by Dec 2017
episodes.summary: On 5 June 2017 Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Egypt cut diplomatic and transport links with Qatar. Onshore, Qatar Central Bank kept supplying dollars at the peg, so the official market never moved. Offshore, where foreign banks and investors deal, liquidity dried up. Several banks stopped quoting or restricted riyal trades, and quotes gapped well below the peg for about six months. Qatar later sued banks, alleging a coordinated campaign against the riyal. The UK FCA found Banque Havilland had drawn up such a plan, though the bank denied trading on it.
precursors: Largely political rather than a macro trigger: reserves and sovereign wealth fund (QIA) assets were very large relative to the monetary base
Gulf banks began pulling deposits and interbank lines from Qatari banks immediately
Oil and LNG prices were low but stable, and the fiscal position was not the driver
episodes.aftermath: The state injected liquidity into banks and redeployed QIA assets, and the offshore rate converged back to the peg by December 2017. The blockade formally ended with the Al-Ula declaration in January 2021.
episodes.hedger_lesson: The peg can hold while your execution price does not. What matters is which rate your NAV, custodian fixing or NDF settlement references, and whether you can reach onshore liquidity through local banks. The offshore dislocation was large but temporary. An investor forced to trade offshore in June–November 2017 crystallised a loss the peg itself never produced.

episodes.title: Saudi Arabia 2015–16: forwards price devaluation, peg holds
episodes.summary: Brent fell from over $100 in mid-2014 to below $30 in January 2016, blowing open Saudi Arabia's fiscal deficit. One-year USD/SAR forward points hit their highest since the late 1990s as funds bet on devaluation. SAMA ran down reserves, borrowed internationally, cut spending, and told banks to stop selling options on riyal forwards. Spot never moved.
precursors: Oil price well below the fiscal breakeven for a sustained period
Rapid drawdown of SAMA net foreign assets
12m forward points rising from near zero (pure carry) to several hundred points
Contagion from other oil-exporter breaks: Kazakhstan (Aug 2015), Azerbaijan (Feb & Dec 2015), Russia (Nov 2014)
episodes.aftermath: Forwards normalised as oil recovered and OPEC+ cut output from late 2016. Saudi Arabia issued a record debut $17.5bn international bond in October 2016.
episodes.hedger_lesson: This was the most intense test of the SAR peg in the modern era, and it held. Forward points were an expensive and noisy signal: shorting SAR via forwards lost the carry. SAMA's options ban also shows the regulator can change the hedging toolkit mid-stress.

episodes.title: Saudi Arabia 2020: price war + pandemic
episodes.summary: The OPEC+ deal collapsed on 6 March 2020, and a Saudi–Russia price war coincided with the pandemic demand shock. Brent roughly halved in March. SAMA's foreign reserves fell by about $27bn in March alone, the fastest pace in at least two decades. The government tripled VAT to 15% and cut spending. The peg was reaffirmed and spot barely moved.
precursors: Fiscal consolidation measures announced under pressure
episodes.aftermath: OPEC+ agreed record cuts in April 2020, oil recovered through 2021, and reserves stabilised.
episodes.hedger_lesson: A second severe oil shock within five years again ended in fiscal adjustment (VAT, spending cuts) rather than devaluation. That is a revealed preference: the kingdom treats the peg as a near-absolute commitment.

episodes.title: Bahrain 2018: weak peg rescued by neighbours
episodes.regime_after: Unchanged, backed by $10bn GCC support package
episodes.summary: Bahrain had the GCC's weakest balance sheet: low reserves, a high debt ratio and a fiscal breakeven far above the oil price. In June 2018, with no sign of Gulf aid, its CDS jumped by a record amount, one-year dinar forwards spiked, and the onshore dinar touched its weakest level in decades. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait then publicly committed support, finalised as a $10bn package later in 2018. Forwards halved within days.
precursors: Reserves covering only weeks of imports
episodes.aftermath: The peg held, with the aid package tied to a fiscal balance programme.
episodes.hedger_lesson: For small GCC pegs, the credible reserves are the neighbours' balance sheets, and the signal to watch is the politics of support. In 2026 the UAE–Bahrain swap line (AED 20bn) is the same mechanism.

episodes.title: GCC 2007–08: pressure to REVALUE
episodes.regime_after: Unchanged (Kuwait had already switched to a basket in May 2007)
episodes.summary: With oil heading to $100+, a weak dollar, Fed rate cuts and Gulf inflation running high, markets bet that the GCC would revalue. Forwards priced appreciation and speculative inflows swelled local liquidity. Kuwait dropped its dollar peg for a basket in May 2007, but the other states held. The 2008 crisis and oil collapse reversed the pressure.
precursors: Imported US monetary easing clashing with overheating local economies
Kuwait's move made the others' commitment less certain
episodes.aftermath: Pegs held. The episode was the mirror image of 2015–16.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Gulf peg risk has run in both directions. For a USD proxy-hedger, a revaluation is a gain, so the risk is asymmetric only if you assume stress is always downward.

episodes.title: Kuwait 2007: dollar peg → basket
episodes.summary: Kuwait abandoned its dollar peg for a basket, citing imported inflation from the weak dollar. The dinar appreciated gradually rather than in a jump. It is the only modern GCC break, and it was upward and orderly.
episodes.aftermath: The basket peg has continued since. KWD is typically much less volatile against USD than a free float.
episodes.hedger_lesson: A GCC 'break' does not have to mean devaluation. A switch to a USD-heavy basket produces modest basis risk against a USD proxy hedge.

episodes.title: Oman 1986: 10% devaluation after oil collapse
episodes.summary: As oil prices collapsed in 1985–86, Oman devalued the rial by about 10% to a new dollar peg rather than floating. That rate has held for 40 years. It is the clearest GCC precedent for what a Gulf break could look like: a one-off step to a new peg.
precursors: Fiscal strain with smaller buffers than Saudi Arabia or Kuwait
episodes.aftermath: The new peg held. Saudi Arabia also formalised a weaker 3.75 parity in 1986 after drifting from about 3.65.
episodes.hedger_lesson: The historical GCC template is a single step devaluation of around 10%, not an EM-style float and collapse. Size tail hedges accordingly, but don't treat that as a cap.

episodes.title: Saudi Arabia 1986: re-peg at 3.75
episodes.regime_before: Managed peg to SDR/USD, drifting weaker (≈3.3–3.65)
episodes.summary: During the early-1980s oil glut, the riyal was allowed to depreciate in small steps from about 3.3 to about 3.65 per dollar. It was fixed at 3.75 in 1986, the rate still in force. Cumulatively this was a managed devaluation spread over several years, not a single overnight break.
precursors: Saudi output cut as swing producer, then the 1986 price collapse
episodes.aftermath: 3.75 has held for 40 years through the 1998, 2015–16, 2020 and 2026 stresses.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Before 1986 the riyal did move under oil stress, gradually. A long-lived peg partly reflects a deliberate choice, made in 1986, to stop adjusting.

episodes.title: Iraq 2020: oil-exporter step devaluation
episodes.regime_after: New peg ~1,450/USD; revalued to ~1,300 in Feb 2023
episodes.summary: Oil provides nearly all of Iraq's fiscal revenue. The 2020 price collapse left the government struggling to pay public salaries, and in December 2020 the central bank devalued by about 18.5% to a new peg rather than floating. In February 2023, amid US restrictions on dollar transfers and a widening parallel premium, it revalued part of the way back.
precursors: Salary arrears and a fiscal financing gap
episodes.aftermath: The official rate was stable at the new level, but a parallel market premium persisted. In 2026, with Hormuz closed and exports cut, the street rate is around 1,545/USD against an official ~1,300–1,320.
episodes.hedger_lesson: The closest recent template for a hydrocarbon-exporter peg break: fiscal, not reserves-driven, and a step to a new peg. Partial reversal is possible too.

datapoints.label: CBI moves official rate from 1,182 to 1,450
Revalued to 1,300
Parallel market ~1,545/USD in Baghdad and Basra

episodes.title: Kazakhstan 2015: oil exporter floats
episodes.summary: The National Bank defended the tenge through the 2014–15 oil collapse, spending reserves and drawing on the oil fund. After Russia floated and China devalued in August 2015, it moved to a free float on 20 August, and the tenge dropped sharply that day. It had already devalued once, by 19%, in February 2014.
precursors: Earlier step devaluation had failed to settle expectations
episodes.aftermath: The tenge kept weakening into early 2016, and banking stress followed.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Large sovereign funds did not prevent a float once the shock looked permanent and competitors had devalued. Kazakhstan's buffers relative to GDP were much smaller than Gulf buffers, though.

datapoints.label: Earlier step devaluation ~19%

episodes.title: Azerbaijan 2015: two-step break
episodes.regime_after: Peg at 1.05, then float from 21 Dec 2015
episodes.summary: Azerbaijan first devalued by about a third to a new dollar peg in February 2015. The new peg lacked credibility, reserves kept draining, and in December 2015 the central bank floated. The manat then fell by roughly another third.
episodes.aftermath: The manat has been re-pegged at 1.70/USD since 2017.
episodes.hedger_lesson: The first devaluation is often not the last. Loss-given-break scenarios should include a second leg.

datapoints.label: Float announced

episodes.title: Russia 2014: band abolished
episodes.summary: Sanctions after Crimea combined with a halving oil price. The central bank, which had been widening its basket corridor, abolished it in November 2014. After the rouble collapse of 16 December, it raised the policy rate to 17% overnight.
precursors: Accelerating reserve sales to defend the corridor
episodes.aftermath: Capital outflows and recession followed. The central bank moved to inflation targeting.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Geopolitical sanctions and an oil shock together can overwhelm large reserves quickly.

episodes.title: Turkmenistan 2015: devaluation, then a parallel market
episodes.summary: A gas exporter hit by falling prices and lost export markets devalued by about 19% to a new peg. The official rate has not moved since, but the street rate diverged to a multiple of it.
episodes.aftermath: The official peg was maintained through rationing, and the parallel market became the true price.
episodes.hedger_lesson: An official rate that never moves can hide a complete break. Watch the parallel premium and access to FX.

episodes.title: Nigeria 2016: float after FX rationing
episodes.summary: After oil collapsed, Nigeria held the official naira rate through 2015–16 by rationing dollars, including barring imports of 41 items from the official FX market. The parallel premium widened, and the central bank moved to a more flexible regime in June 2016.
precursors: Foreign portfolio investors trapped by repatriation backlogs
episodes.aftermath: Multiple exchange-rate windows followed, with a further unification and large devaluation in June 2023.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Before the price broke, access broke. Foreign investors faced repatriation queues, and NDFs traded well away from the official rate.

datapoints.label: Further unification and devaluation

episodes.title: Libya 2021: unification with the 'real' rate
episodes.regime_before: Official ~1.4 LYD/USD plus FX surcharge; parallel market
episodes.regime_after: Unified 4.48/USD; devalued again to ~5.57 in Apr 2025
episodes.summary: Civil conflict and oil blockades had left Libya with a fictional official rate, a surcharge rate for most transactions, and a parallel market. In January 2021 the central bank unified at 4.48/USD. The headline move was more than 200%, but for most real transactions the effective change was far smaller. A further 13% devaluation followed in April 2025.
episodes.aftermath: Relative stability until the 2025 devaluation.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Headline break size depends on which rate you were marked at. With multiple rates, the break can be mostly accounting.

datapoints.label: Devalued ~13% to ~5.57/USD

episodes.title: Bolivia 2026: 15-year peg ends
episodes.summary: Bolivia's gas exports declined and reserves fell from over $15bn to under $2bn, much of the remainder in gold. The official rate stayed at 6.96 while dollars became scarce and the parallel market priced the boliviano far weaker. The new government announced unification in May 2026 and started the float on 29 June at 9.73. The rate reached about 12.6 in early September.
precursors: Change of government with a reform mandate
episodes.aftermath: Volatile float with IMF talks. The official move was a partial catch-up to the parallel market.
episodes.hedger_lesson: The parallel premium was the loudest and longest-running signal. Reserves-to-short-term-needs ran down for years before the break.

datapoints.label: FX unification announced
Float begins at 9.73/USD

episodes.title: Lebanon 2019–23: the peg that 'held' while depositors lost 90%
episodes.regime_after: Official held until Feb 2023 (15,000); converged to ~89,500 by 2024
episodes.summary: Lebanon's peg was financed by attracting dollar deposits at ever-higher rates, which some described as a Ponzi scheme. When inflows stopped in 2019, banks closed during the October protests and imposed informal capital controls. The official 1,507.5 rate stayed on the books for more than three years while street rates reached tens of thousands, and trapped 'lollar' deposits could only be withdrawn at punitive rates.
precursors: Twin deficits financed by deposit inflows
Central bank 'financial engineering' paying very high rates for dollars
Emergence of a parallel rate before October 2019
episodes.aftermath: Eurobond default in March 2020, banking system insolvency, and hyperinflation-level currency collapse.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Measured by the official rate, the peg never broke until 2023. Measured by what a foreign investor could actually repatriate, it broke in 2019. A hedge settling on the official fixing would have paid nothing. Convertibility and transfer risk are separate from rate risk.

datapoints.label: Banks close amid protests; informal capital controls follow
Eurobond default
Official rate moved to 15,000

episodes.title: Egypt 2016: float after parallel-market squeeze
episodes.summary: Reserves were depleted and dollars rationed, and the parallel rate reached roughly double the official one. Egypt floated in November 2016 as part of a $12bn IMF programme, and the pound roughly halved in value within weeks.
episodes.aftermath: Carry-trade inflows followed, and the pattern repeated in 2022 (March and October) and March 2024.
episodes.hedger_lesson: A recurring pattern: official peg, rationing, parallel premium, IMF deal, then float. The parallel premium sets the likely magnitude.

episodes.title: Egypt 2024: Gulf money finances the break
episodes.summary: The UAE's roughly $35bn Ras El-Hekma investment in February 2024 and an enlarged IMF programme gave the central bank enough dollars to let the official rate jump to the parallel level. After that, the parallel market largely disappeared.
episodes.aftermath: The rate unified and stabilised.
episodes.hedger_lesson: External money can make a break orderly. It paid for the break rather than preventing it.

episodes.title: Switzerland 2015: floor removed without warning
episodes.summary: The SNB removed its minimum exchange rate on 15 January 2015, days after officials had called it a cornerstone of policy, ahead of expected ECB QE. EUR/CHF gapped far below parity intraday, liquidity vanished, and several retail FX brokers failed or needed rescue.
episodes.aftermath: The franc settled ~10–15% stronger. Negative rates followed.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Gap risk: stop-loss or trigger-based hedging does not execute at the peg. A central bank reaffirming days before is not evidence either way. This is the case for holding some protection ahead of time rather than planning to trade on the news.

episodes.title: Czech Republic 2017: telegraphed floor exit
episodes.summary: The Czech National Bank signalled its exit for months, then ended the floor in April 2017. Despite large speculative long-koruna positions, the currency appreciated only modestly and in an orderly way.
precursors: Explicit forward guidance on exit timing
episodes.aftermath: Gradual appreciation.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Contrast with CHF: telegraphed, strong-side exits rarely gap.

episodes.title: Denmark 2015: peg defended against appreciation
episodes.summary: After the SNB's move, markets tested the krone peg. Danmarks Nationalbank cut its deposit rate four times in under three weeks to −0.75%, intervened heavily and suspended government bond issuance. The peg held within a very narrow range.
episodes.aftermath: Inflows reversed within months.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Strong-side pressure can be resisted almost indefinitely, because a central bank can print its own currency. Weak-side defences are limited by reserves.

episodes.title: Hong Kong 1997–98: currency board survives the 'double play'
episodes.summary: During the Asian crisis, speculators shorted both HKD and Hong Kong equities, betting that the rate spike needed to defend the board would crash stocks. Overnight HIBOR spiked to around 280% in October 1997. In August 1998 the HKMA bought about HK$118bn of equities to break the strategy.
episodes.aftermath: The peg held with a deep recession and property crash. It was later tested on the weak side in 2022–23.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Currency boards defend with interest rates, so peg stress can show up in local rates and asset prices before spot moves. Watch interbank spreads to the anchor.

datapoints.label: Overnight HIBOR spikes (~280%)

episodes.title: Hong Kong 1983: a peg as the cure
episodes.summary: Uncertainty over Sino-British negotiations drove a run on the floating HKD ('Black Saturday', 24 September 1983). Adopting the linked rate at 7.80 stopped it. The rate has been in place for over 40 years.
episodes.aftermath: One of the longest-lived hard pegs.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Pegs are often adopted after a crisis. Longevity reflects the institutional commitment built afterwards.

datapoints.label: Black Saturday

episodes.title: Thailand 1997: forward book exhausted, onshore/offshore split
episodes.summary: The Bank of Thailand defended the baht largely through forward-market swaps, so headline reserves looked healthy while most were committed. In May 1997 it split the market, limiting non-residents' access to onshore baht. Offshore rates and yields diverged sharply from onshore, a precursor of Qatar 2017. It floated on 2 July, setting off the Asian crisis.
precursors: Reserves committed in forward swaps (disclosed only after the float)
episodes.aftermath: Contagion to Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Korea, and an IMF programme.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Headline reserves can overstate defensive capacity. Look for forward and swap books, and treat a new onshore/offshore wedge as a late-stage warning.

datapoints.label: Two-tier market: non-resident access to baht restricted

episodes.title: Indonesia 1997: band abandoned, free fall
episodes.summary: Indonesia widened its crawling band after Thailand floated, then abandoned it on 14 August 1997. Corporate dollar debt, a banking collapse and political crisis turned the depreciation into the deepest of the Asian crisis.
episodes.aftermath: IMF programmes, bank closures, and regime change in 1998.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Loss-given-break depends on balance-sheet mismatches. When the private sector is short dollars, a break feeds on itself.

episodes.title: Korea 1997: band abolished
episodes.summary: Korea's short-term external debt far exceeded usable reserves, much of which had been lent to banks. The Bank of Korea stopped defending 1,000/USD on 17 November 1997, widened the daily band on 20 November, agreed an IMF package in early December and abolished the band on 16 December. Dated here from the end of the defence, when most of the fall began.
episodes.aftermath: V-shaped recovery from 1999.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Short-term external debt against usable (not headline) reserves was the clearest red flag.

episodes.title: Malaysia 1998: re-peg with capital controls
episodes.regime_after: Peg 3.80/USD with capital controls until Jul 2005
episodes.summary: After a year of floating, Malaysia pegged at 3.80, imposed controls on capital outflows and made offshore ringgit worthless by requiring it to be repatriated. The offshore ringgit market, centred in Singapore, was shut down.
precursors: Offshore ringgit borrowing used to short the currency
episodes.aftermath: The peg held for seven years, with controls gradually relaxed.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Policy can close the offshore market by decree. Offshore NDF and deliverable hedges carry the risk of the market disappearing.

episodes.title: Mexico 1994: the Tequila crisis
episodes.summary: Political shocks drained reserves through 1994 as the government replaced peso debt with dollar-indexed tesobonos. The band was widened on 20 December and the peso floated two days later.
episodes.aftermath: US-led ~$50bn rescue.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Anchor-country tightening (the Fed in 1994) can be the trigger.

episodes.title: Russia 1998: default and devaluation
episodes.summary: With oil near $12, persistent fiscal deficits and short-term GKO debt, Russia widened its band, defaulted on domestic debt and declared a moratorium on foreign payments on 17 August 1998. The rouble floated in early September.
episodes.aftermath: LTCM collapse and global contagion.
episodes.hedger_lesson: In an oil-exporter break with default, settlement risk on local-currency forwards became real: several NDF counterparties disputed payment.

episodes.title: Brazil 1999: crawling peg collapses
episodes.summary: Despite an IMF package in late 1998, fiscal doubts and Minas Gerais' debt moratorium triggered outflows. Brazil devalued on 13 January 1999 and floated two days later.
episodes.aftermath: Moved to inflation targeting and recovered faster than feared.
episodes.hedger_lesson: An IMF backstop reduced tail severity but did not prevent the break.

episodes.title: Argentina 2002: currency board collapse
episodes.regime_after: Dual rate, then float from Feb 2002
episodes.summary: A legally entrenched 1:1 currency board failed after three years of recession, a strong dollar and a devalued Brazilian real. Deposits were frozen from December 2001 (the corralito). The sovereign defaulted, convertibility was repealed on 6 January 2002, and the peso lost around three-quarters of its value within months.
precursors: Real appreciation vs trading partners (Brazil's 1999 devaluation)
episodes.aftermath: Asymmetric 'pesification' of dollar contracts, and a deep depression before recovery.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Even the hardest legal peg broke when fiscal and banking systems failed. Convertibility risk arrived before price risk, and contracts were rewritten by decree.

datapoints.label: Corralito deposit freeze

episodes.title: Turkey 2001: crawling peg abandoned
episodes.summary: Banking fragility caused a liquidity crisis in November 2000. A political row in February 2001 set off a run, overnight rates spiked to several thousand percent, and Turkey floated on 22 February.
episodes.aftermath: Large IMF programme and banking restructuring.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Extreme spikes in the interbank rate are a late-stage but reliable signal that a defence is failing.

episodes.title: UK 1992: Black Wednesday
episodes.summary: After reunification the Bundesbank kept rates high while Britain was in recession. On 16 September 1992 the Bank of England raised rates from 10% to 12% and announced 15%, then suspended ERM membership that evening.
precursors: Anchor central bank tightening into a local downturn
Finland and Italy pegs failing days earlier
episodes.aftermath: The UK recovered with lower rates, and the exit is widely seen as having been beneficial.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Relevant to 2026: a peg imports the anchor's monetary policy. When the Fed tightens into a local downturn, as in Qatar and Kuwait, defending the peg gets politically costlier even with reserves. The Gulf's hard commitment and lack of domestic inflation targeting make it very different, though.

episodes.title: Italy 1992: ERM exit
episodes.summary: Italy devalued within the ERM on 13 September 1992, but the realignment failed to stop the run, and the lira left the ERM four days later.
episodes.aftermath: Re-entered the ERM in 1996 and joined the euro.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Another two-step break: the initial realignment was not enough.

episodes.title: Sweden 1992: 500% rates, then float
episodes.summary: In the middle of a banking crisis, the Riksbank raised its marginal lending rate to 500% in September 1992 and defended the krona for two more months, then floated on 19 November.
episodes.aftermath: Adopted inflation targeting, and the recovery was strong.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Extreme rate defences can buy time but rarely save a peg that the domestic economy cannot bear.

episodes.title: Finland 1992: markka floats
episodes.summary: The collapse of Soviet trade and a banking crisis led to a devaluation in November 1991 and a float in September 1992.
precursors: Loss of a major export market
episodes.aftermath: Deep recession, then recovery.
episodes.hedger_lesson: A sudden loss of export markets for structural reasons (compare Qatar's Hormuz-blocked LNG) is a classic trigger, but Finland lacked Gulf-style buffers.

episodes.title: UK 1967: Bretton Woods devaluation
episodes.summary: After years of balance-of-payments strain, repeated sterling crises and reserve losses, the UK devalued by 14.3% to a new peg.
episodes.aftermath: The new peg held until Bretton Woods collapsed.
episodes.hedger_lesson: In the fixed-rate era a devaluation was a single step to a new peg, the template GCC breaks would most likely follow.

episodes.title: China 2015: surprise fixing reform
episodes.summary: The PBoC changed the daily fixing mechanism, and the renminbi fell about 3% within days. The move triggered global risk-off and capital outflows, and China spent roughly $1tn of reserves over 2014–16.
episodes.aftermath: Capital controls were tightened.
episodes.hedger_lesson: Small moves in systemic pegs can have large spillovers. This one hit other oil and EM pegs, including Kazakhstan nine days later.

episodes.title: Ukraine 2014: war and float
episodes.summary: Political upheaval, then war in the east, overwhelmed low reserves. The hryvnia was allowed to float in February 2014 and lost about two-thirds of its value within a year.
episodes.aftermath: IMF programmes and capital controls.
episodes.hedger_lesson: War and geopolitical shocks break pegs quickly when buffers are thin. Gulf buffers are the key difference in 2026.

episodes.title: Sri Lanka 2022: reserves run out
episodes.summary: Tax cuts, loss of tourism and a debt overhang drained reserves. The rupee was held flat for months with FX rationing before being floated in March 2022. Sovereign default followed in April.
episodes.aftermath: Default, IMF programme and debt restructuring.
episodes.hedger_lesson: A rate held flat by rationing is a warning sign, not stability.

episodes.title: Ethiopia 2024: float to close parallel gap
episodes.summary: As part of an IMF programme, Ethiopia let the birr float, and the official rate moved toward the parallel market within weeks.
episodes.aftermath: Converged toward the parallel rate.
episodes.hedger_lesson: The parallel premium sets the magnitude again.
